plan.contextChunk: This figure is a grouped vertical bar chart on a pale blue plotting field comparing two thermal properties of the straight-chain alkanes. The horizontal axis, labeled Number of carbons, carries fourteen categories numbered 1 through 14. The vertical axis, labeled Temperature (degrees C), runs from -200 at the bottom to 300 at the top with labeled gridlines every 100 degrees, and the bars grow upward or downward from the zero gridline. A legend in the upper left assigns blue to Melting point and magenta to Boiling point, and each carbon number carries one bar of each color, blue on the left and magenta on the right. Both series climb steadily from left to right. The blue melting-point bars begin near -180 at one carbon and stay below zero until the last two categories, where they finally reach and just cross the zero line. The magenta boiling-point bars start near -165, rise past zero at four carbons, and continue to roughly 250 at fourteen carbons. In every pair the magenta bar stands taller than the blue one, and the vertical gap between the two widens toward the right of the chart. The plot backs the observation that both transition temperatures increase with molecular size, since the dispersion forces holding molecules together grow as the chain lengthens.

interactionPlan.concept: The melting and boiling points of straight-chain alkanes increase steadily as the carbon chain lengthens because larger molecules have stronger intermolecular dispersion forces.

demo_steps.title: Increasing dispersion forces
demo_steps.narration: As the carbon chain gets longer, both transition temperatures generally rise because larger surface areas create stronger intermolecular dispersion forces holding the molecules together.

demo_steps.title: Boiling points and gases
demo_steps.narration: Focusing on boiling points, notice they cross 0°C at just 4 carbons (butane). This means alkanes with 1 to 4 carbons boil below room temperature and are gases.

demo_steps.title: Melting points and solids
demo_steps.narration: Melting points stay much lower. They remain below 0°C until the chain reaches 14 carbons, meaning alkanes only become solid at room temperature when the chains are quite long.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Both melting and boiling points increase with chain length due to dispersion forces, but boiling points are always higher and cross typical room temperatures at much shorter chain lengths.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Grouped vertical bar chart. Ensure the 0°C baseline is clearly visible, as bars for lower carbon counts extend downwards (negative) from this line, while others extend upwards. Blue bars are positioned on the left of each pair, magenta on the right. Maintain the specific crossing points: magenta crosses 0 at x=4, blue crosses 0 at x=14. The gap between the magenta and blue bars generally widens as the carbon count increases.

authoredContext:
Alkanes show regular increases in both boiling point and melting point as molecular weight increases (the figure), an effect due to the presence of weak dispersion forces between molecules (another section). Only when sufficient energy is applied to overcome these forces does the solid melt or liquid boil. As you might expect, dispersion forces increase as molecular size increases, accounting for the higher melting and boiling points of larger alkanes.

A plot of melting and boiling points versus number of carbon atoms for the C1–C14 straight-chain alkanes. There is a regular increase with molecular size.

A double bar graph of temperature versus the number of carbon atoms that plots bars for melting and boiling points with an increasing trend.

Another effect seen in alkanes is that increased branching lowers an alkane’s boiling point. Thus, pentane has no branches and boils at 36.1 °C, isopentane (2-methylbutane) has one branch and boils at 27.85 °C, and neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane) has two branches and boils at 9.5 °C. Similarly, octane boils at 125.7 °C, whereas isooctane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) boils at 99.3 °C. Branched-chain alkanes are lower-boiling because they are more nearly spherical than straight-chain alkanes, have smaller surface areas, and consequently have smaller dispersion forces.
